Guinean sea catfish Carlarius parkii attains a maximum recorded total length of 75 centimeters [Li = 75 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger ariids inhabiting the coastal waters of West Africa. This ultimate length is achieved through a protracted growth phase that spans much of the species' life, with individuals accumulating considerable somatic mass as they mature. Field surveys conducted in estuarine environments along the Gulf of Guinea indicate that the largest specimens are typically captured at depths of ten to thirty meters, where prey resources are abundant. The species exhibits a robust, elongate body form typical of marine catfishes, with a broad head and prominent barbels that aid in benthic foraging. Sexual dimorphism in maximum size appears limited, although gravid females occasionally reach slightly greater lengths than males of equivalent age. The condition factor of these large adults suggests good nutritional status, reflecting the productivity of the inshore habitats they occupy. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Carlarius heudelotii indicate that a maximum length of 75 centimeters [Li = 75 centimeters] is broadly consistent within the genus, though local environmental conditions modulate growth trajectories.

Puberty in this species occurs when individuals reach a total length of 32 centimeters [Lp = 32 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal development and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from specimens collected in the Bijagós Archipelago revealed that oocyte maturation commences at this size, with vitellogenesis becoming evident in females exceeding this length. The body mass associated with this developmental milestone has been estimated at 328 grams [Wwp = 328 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from a large dataset spanning multiple years. This weight at puberty represents a substantial increase from the neonatal stage, reflecting the accumulation of somatic resources necessary to support initial reproductive investment. Males appear to reach sexual maturity at a slightly smaller size than females, a pattern common among ariid catfishes where females invest more heavily in egg production. The length at puberty of 32 centimeters [Lp = 32 centimeters] aligns well with estimates for other members of the Ariidae family that occupy similar tropical estuarine niches.

Reproductive output in Carlarius parkii is tightly linked to thermal conditions, with the maximum spawning rate observed at 9.4 °C [T = 9.4 °C] during the cooler upwelling months off the coast of Sierra Leone. Under these conditions, females produce approximately 71 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 71 eggs per spawning event], with approximately 365 spawning events each year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events each year]. The daily reproductive rate derived from these parameters reflects the species' relatively low fecundity compared to many marine teleosts, a pattern associated with the production of large, yolk-rich eggs that undergo extensive parental care. This reproductive strategy is characteristic of ariids, where males engage in oral incubation of the developing embryos. The selection of cooler spawning temperatures likely enhances offspring survival by reducing metabolic demands on the brooding male and increasing oxygen availability to the developing eggs within the buccal cavity. Field observations indicate that spawning aggregations form in shallow, well-oxygenated waters during the peak of the upwelling season.

Neonatal mass at birth is remarkably low for a fish of this ultimate size, with newly released young weighing approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams] based on an average egg diameter of 1.5 millimeters. This extraordinary weight reflects the production of small, well-yolked eggs that develop rapidly within the male's buccal cavity before release as free-swimming juveniles. The developing embryos rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves throughout incubation, with the male providing only physical protection and aeration. Following release, the yolk-sac larvae exhibit lecithotrophic nutrition for several days before transitioning to exogenous feeding on small zooplankton. The wet weight at birth of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams] contrasts sharply with the ultimate wet weight of 4,400 grams (4400 grams) [Wwi = 4400 grams] attained by fully grown adults, representing a mass increase of more than two million-fold over the life cycle. This extreme ontogenetic trajectory underscores the species' capacity for rapid juvenile growth in productive coastal ecosystems.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Carlarius parkii in natural populations is 10 years [am = 10 years] under the thermal regime typical of tropical West African waters, where mean annual temperatures average 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C]. This longevity is comparable to that of other large ariid catfishes and reflects a life-history strategy characterized by delayed maturity, moderate fecundity, and extended parental investment. The ultimate wet weight of 4,400 grams (4400 grams) [Wwi = 4400 grams] is achieved gradually over this decadal lifespan, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of reproductive maturity. Senescence-related mortality becomes apparent in individuals exceeding eight years of age, with field observations noting increased incidence of parasitic infections and reduced condition factor in the oldest age classes. The combination of a 10-year lifespan (10 years) [am = 10 years] and a moderate reproductive output suggests a relatively stable population dynamics, buffered against environmental stochasticity by the iteroparous spawning strategy and extended parental care that enhance juvenile survival at a temperature of 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C]. Ongoing climate change may alter these demographic parameters as water temperatures in the region continue to rise.
